megh-007.title: Mount St. Helens lays down its Yn tephra
megh-007.text: Long before the blast described in {{ref:megh-102}}, Mount St. Helens had a far larger eruption. About 1860 BCE it laid down its Yn, or Smith Creek, tephra in a VEI 6 eruption of roughly 15 km³. That layer of ash is part of the volcano's long record of violent eruptions.

megh-023.title: The Homeric solar minimum
megh-023.text: For about two centuries, the Sun went quiet. A deep, persistent grand solar minimum, the Homeric Minimum, lasted from about 800 to 600 BC. It is linked to the Homeric Climate Oscillation, or 2.8 kyr event, when western North America and Europe grew colder. Whether they also grew wetter or drier is debated. Germany's Meerfelder Maar records a lasting shift to colder, wetter, windier weather. The Göschenen I glacier advance in the Alps relates to it.

megh-063.title: The 1700 Cascadia earthquake and its orphan tsunami
megh-063.text: Around 9 pm on 26 January 1700, a magnitude 9.0 earthquake ruptured the 1,000 km Cascadia subduction zone off North America's Pacific coast. A subduction zone is where one tectonic plate dives beneath another. Coasts from British Columbia to Oregon dropped up to 2 m and were buried by tsunami sand, leaving drowned ghost forests. Drowned red cedars in Oregon and Washington have outermost rings from 1699, the last growing season before the earthquake. The tsunami crossed the Pacific and struck Honshu, Japan, about ten hours later. There it was recorded as an orphan tsunami, a wave with no felt earthquake. Oral traditions of several coastal peoples recall earthquakes and saltwater floods. It remains the zone's last megathrust earthquake.

megh-065.title: Methane climbs 2.6-fold
megh-065.text: Methane makes up just 3% of greenhouse emissions by mass, but about 23% of climate forcing. Since about 1750, atmospheric methane rose from 722 ppb to 1,936 ppb by 2025. That 2.6-fold increase is the highest level in at least 800,000 years, and human activities caused almost all of it. After a decade of near-zero growth, methane began climbing again in 2007, with sharp rises in 2015–2019 and a record annual jump in 2021. Isotopes suggest recent growth comes mainly from microbial sources such as wetlands and agriculture rather than fossil fuels. From 2010 to 2019, methane caused about 0.5 °C, roughly 30%, of observed global warming.

megh-066.title: The Great Lisbon earthquake
megh-066.text: On 1 November 1755 the Great Lisbon earthquake struck, killing around 100,000 people. It was one of the most destructive earthquakes in history. It heads the list of large earthquakes and tsunamis the Azores–Gibraltar fault zone has produced since records began in the 1700s.

megh-067.title: Steller's sea cow: gone in 27 years
megh-067.text: Steller's sea cow was the largest known sirenian, a plant-eating sea mammal, at up to 10 m and 5–10 tonnes. It survived as a relict in the Bering Sea's Commander Islands. Discovered in 1741, it was hunted for meat and hides until it was gone by 1768, just 27 years later.

megh-068.title: The Industrial Revolution starts the greenhouse rise
megh-068.text: For 10,000 years before the mid-18th century, carbon dioxide stayed near 280 ppm. It has since risen 54%. The turn came with the Industrial Revolution, around 1780 and the steam engine, when large-scale greenhouse gas emissions began to warm Earth. Antarctic ice cores record the highest greenhouse gas levels from the Industrial Revolution on. The IPCC takes 1750 as its pre-industrial baseline. Warm decades became more common. Recorded extinctions mounted too: over 322 species are often cited as lost to humans since then, a toll followed in {{ref:megh-079}}. The Industrial Revolution is one proposed start of the Anthropocene, though humans had already reshaped much of Earth's landscape. Its gases set up the changes of {{ref:megh-090}} and {{ref:megh-093}}.

megh-069.title: The Laki fissure poisons Iceland
megh-069.text: About a fifth of Iceland's people died after the Laki eruption. From June 1783 to February 1784, the 40 km Laki fissure poured out about 15 km³ of lava, one of history's largest effusive eruptions, those that pour lava rather than explode. Its lava fields cover 565 km² of southeast Iceland. Fluorine and chlorine poisoning devastated farming. The eruption released about 120 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide. In Northern Hemisphere ice cores its sulfate signal exceeds even that of Samalas, and the sulfur caused substantial cooling. Famine cost Egypt a sixth of its people in 1784, and hardship in Europe may have fed the French Revolution.

megh-071.title: Tambora, the most powerful eruption on record
megh-071.text: On 10 April 1815, an eruption column rose 45 km over the Indonesian island of Sumbawa. Tambora was at its climax. Its eruption that April was the most powerful in recorded history, a VEI 7 that ejected 37–45 km³ of material. It is also the most recent confirmed VEI-7 eruption. About 10,000–11,000 people died directly. Another 49,000–90,000 died from famine and disease on Sumbawa, Lombok and Bali. The eruption's reach went far beyond the islands. Its sulfur dioxide formed a stratospheric sulfate veil, a haze of fine droplets high above the weather. In 1815 people saw it as a persistent dry fog that dimmed the Sun. That veil brought the global chill described in {{ref:megh-072}}.

megh-072.title: 1816, the Year Without a Summer
megh-072.text: Frost and snow struck New England and Quebec in June 1816, ruining most North American crops. Tambora's aerosols had lowered global temperatures by about 0.4–0.7 °C, and 1816 became the Year Without a Summer across the Northern Hemisphere. Harvests failed across Europe in the worst famine of the nineteenth century. India's monsoon failed, and a new cholera strain spread from Bengal. 1816 was the Northern Hemisphere's second-coldest year since about 1400. The 1810s were the coldest decade on record, aided by an eruption around 1809. The cold also fell during the Dalton Minimum, a period of unusually low solar radiation.

megh-073.title: The 1831 eruption traced to Zavaritski Caldera
megh-073.text: A high-magnitude explosive eruption in the northern summer of 1831 may have come from Zavaritski Caldera on Simushir, in the Kuril Islands. Its reconstructed radiative forcing, its effect on Earth's energy balance, matches that of Pinatubo in 1991. It may explain cooling in 1831–1833, which ended the volcanic cold spell of 1809–1831.

megh-075.title: Glaciers retreat as the Little Ice Age ends
megh-075.text: By 1879 the ice of Alaska's Glacier Bay had retreated 77 km. Glaciers began a strong retreat after about 1850, as the Little Ice Age ended in the late nineteenth century. Since 1850 Austria has lost 40% of its glacier cover and Switzerland 30%, and Pyrenean glaciers have also retreated greatly. Alpine glaciers shrank from 1,817 km² in 1876 to 1,342 km² by 1973, reducing river run-off. Photographs show the retreat clearly. Only 27% of Glacier National Park's 1850 ice cover remained by 1993.

megh-076.title: Modern sea-level rise begins
megh-076.text: For the last 3,000 years, sea level was nearly stable. Then its rise accelerated, an onset variously dated between 1850 and 1900. Tide gauges, later joined by satellites, show global mean sea level rose 19.5 cm between 1870 and 2004, about 1.44 mm a year. Between 1901 and 2018 it rose 15–25 cm, faster than in any century for at least 4,000 years. Since the 1970s it has climbed 2.3 mm a year, a pace that quickens in {{ref:megh-106}}.

megh-078.title: Krakatoa explodes
megh-078.text: The blasts were heard 4,800 km away on Rodrigues. On 26–27 August 1883, Krakatoa, in Indonesia's Sunda Strait, exploded in one of history's most violent eruptions, VEI 6, ejecting about 25 km³ of rock. Barographs worldwide recorded its pressure wave seven times as it circled the globe. Tsunamis with a 41 m run-up killed at least 36,417 people, and two-thirds of the island was destroyed, leaving a caldera. Ash rose 80 km, and Northern Hemisphere summer temperatures fell by an average of 0.4 °C that year. The sterilised islands became a classic case of ecosystems rebuilding from scratch. From 1927, Anak Krakatau rose from the caldera.

megh-079.title: Extinctions soar above the background rate
megh-079.text: Since 1900, extinctions have run at over 1,000 times the background rate, the normal pace of extinction, and the rate is still rising. Humanity has entered what is sometimes called Earth's sixth major extinction, at perhaps 100 to 1,000 times the background rate, though the exact rate is disputed. Over 322 species are often cited as lost to human activity since the Industrial Revolution, perhaps 500 vertebrates alone, mostly after 1900. Islands suffer most: 95% of bird extinctions since the late 15th century were of island species, as the dodo of {{ref:megh-062}} showed early on.

megh-080.title: Santa María erupts in Guatemala
megh-080.text: In October 1902, Santa María in Guatemala had its first recorded eruption. The VEI 6 blast ejected about 5.5 km³ of magma over two days, and 7,000–13,000 people died. It ranks with Novarupta (1912) and Pinatubo (1991) among the three largest eruptions of the 20th century.

megh-081.title: The Tunguska explosion flattens a Siberian forest
megh-081.text: On 30 June 1908, a huge explosion over the Siberian taiga near the Podkamennaya Tunguska River flattened about 2,150 km² of forest. Scientists attribute it to the air burst of a 50–60 m meteoroid 5–10 km up, releasing about 10–15 megatons. Whether the body was an asteroid or a comet is debated. The shock wave killed at least three people and was detected worldwide, and bright nights followed across western Eurasia. Models suggest it made nitric oxide that cut ozone by 35–45% in early 1909. It is the most violent impact event recorded in modern times. Nearby Lake Cheko may be a fragment's crater, though sediment studies disagree.

megh-082.title: Novarupta, the 20th century's largest eruption
megh-082.text: Beginning 6 June 1912, Novarupta on the Alaska Peninsula produced the 20th century's largest eruption. The 60-hour VEI 6 blast threw out 13–15 km³ of ash. Magma drained from beneath Mount Katmai, whose summit collapsed. Deep pyroclastic flows filled the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes. No one died directly, but the most ash-buried Native villages were abandoned.

megh-083.title: Martha, the last passenger pigeon
megh-083.text: The passenger pigeon was once perhaps 40% of all birds in North America. Habitat loss and mass hunting for a meat industry destroyed it. It was declared extinct in 1914, when Martha, the last known bird, died at the Cincinnati Zoo. The species had vanished from the wild 20 years before.

megh-084.title: The last thylacine dies in Hobart
megh-084.text: The thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, was a dog-like marsupial predator. After {{ref:megh-017}} it survived only in Tasmania, and the last confirmed wild one was killed in 1931. The last known thylacine died at Hobart Zoo on 7 September 1936. A 2023 analysis of sightings suggests it may have lingered for decades.

megh-086.title: Iron rains on Sikhote-Alin
megh-086.text: On 12 February 1947, an iron meteorite of over 23 tonnes fell in the Sikhote-Alin Mountains of the Soviet Far East. It broke apart as it fell. Its fragments scattered over about 1.3 km² and blasted craters up to 26 m across.

megh-088.title: Is the Atlantic overturning slowing?
megh-088.text: The Atlantic meridional overturning circulation carries warm surface water north. Reconstructions suggest that by 2015 it was weaker than before the Industrial Revolution, by roughly 15–20% since the mid-twentieth century. One analysis found it weaker in 1975–1995 than at any time in the past millennium. Ocean warming and Greenland meltwater may be weakening it. Yet some studies find no overall decline, and how much is natural variability is debated.

megh-089.title: The ocean turns more acidic
megh-089.text: Between 1950 and 2026, average ocean-surface pH fell from about 8.15 to 8.05. That small-looking drop is roughly a 26% rise in hydrogen-ion concentration, the measure of acidity. Human carbon dioxide is the main cause: from 1850 to 2022 the ocean absorbed 26% of all anthropogenic emissions. Present-day surface pH, and its rate of change, are unprecedented for at least 26,000 years. Interior ocean pH has also fallen everywhere over the last 20–30 years. Falling pH lowers carbonate saturation. That speeds dissolution of the calcium carbonate that molluscs, foraminifera and other shell-builders need.

megh-090.title: Rapid global warming since the mid-20th century
megh-090.text: The global average temperature was 14 °C for 1951–1980 and 15 °C for 2013–2017. One degree may sound small, but it is an average over the whole planet. Greenhouse gases from fossil fuels have caused this planetary-scale climate change. Warm decades became ever more common after {{ref:megh-068}}. The ocean is about 0.7 °C warmer than in 1950, and that warming has contributed more than 15 cm of sea-level rise. The heat is not spread evenly. The Arctic warmed faster than most regions, and land twice as fast as ocean. Antarctica warmed after 1957, and the South Pole warmed at triple the global rate after 1990. The effects reach every part of the Earth system. They include more extreme weather, thawing permafrost, marine heatwaves, ocean deoxygenation and acidification, as {{ref:megh-089}} shows.

megh-091.title: The 1952 Kamchatka earthquake
megh-091.text: Waves 15–18 m high struck Severo-Kurilsk on 5 November 1952. A magnitude 8.8–9.0 megathrust earthquake had struck off Kamchatka, one of the four most powerful quakes measured since the 1930s. It ruptured the Kuril–Kamchatka subduction zone, which has produced several giant quakes, including those of 1737 and 2025. Just after the quake, Tao-Rusyr Caldera in the Kuril Islands had its only historical eruption, building a small lava dome. The quake remains Russia's most powerful recorded, fifth worldwide since 1900. Its tsunami, which struck the Kuril Islands and Kamchatka, was Russia's deadliest and most damaging.

megh-092.title: The Great Acceleration and the bomb spike
megh-092.text: In the sediments of Crawford Lake, Ontario, a thin layer records a plutonium spike from hydrogen-bomb tests at 1952. Alongside it lie carbon particles and nitrates from fossil fuels and fertilizers. They mark the Great Acceleration: after World War II, population, economic growth, pollution and resource use all began rising at a dramatic rate. Since about 1950 humans have doubled Earth's fixed nitrogen. They have opened an ozone hole with CFCs and cut off almost a fifth of river sediment from the sea. Atomic-bomb tests scattered radionuclides, radioactive forms of elements, around the globe. Caesium-137, strontium-90 and plutonium settled into sediments and glacial ice. Global radionuclide levels peaked around 1965, and bomb carbon-14 entered atmospheric CO2 and the biosphere. These traces were proposed as a marker for a new epoch, a proposal settled in {{ref:megh-123}}.

megh-094.title: West Antarctica warms and sheds ice
megh-094.text: West Antarctica warmed by about 2.4 °C between 1958 and 2012, a change attributed to rising greenhouse gases. Warming seawater melts its ice shelves from below. Its coastal glaciers, above all Thwaites, Pine Island and Smith, have retreated substantially since at least the 1990s. Ice loss rose from 53 Gt a year in 1992 to 159 Gt a year in 2017, adding about 7.6 mm to global sea level.

megh-093.title: The Keeling Curve climbs at Mauna Loa
megh-093.text: On 9 May 2013, daily carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa passed 400 ppm. That level was probably not reached since the mid-Pliocene, 2 to 4 million years ago. Continuous measurements there began in March 1958 and gave the first significant evidence of rapidly rising atmospheric CO2. The record climbed steadily from 313 ppm in March 1958 to 406 ppm in November 2018. By then it was rising about 2.5 ppm a year. Air in ice cores shows Holocene CO2 stayed between 275 and 285 ppm until it began rising sharply early in the nineteenth century. The accelerating rise comes from burning fossil fuels. The curve also swings about 6 ppm each year with Northern Hemisphere plant growth.

megh-095.title: Valdivia 1960: the largest earthquake ever recorded
megh-095.text: The largest earthquake ever recorded, of moment magnitude 9.4–9.6, struck southern Chile on 22 May 1960. It ruptured the subduction zone where the Nazca plate sinks beneath southern Chile, a boundary with a long history of massive earthquakes. Its tsunami reached 25 m on the Chilean coast and 10.7 m at Hilo, Hawaii, 10,000 km away. Between 1,000 and 6,000 people died. Two days after the main shock, the Cordón Caulle volcano began erupting along its southern flank. Similar great earthquakes struck the region in 1575 and around 1800 BC, the latter dated from tsunami debris in the Atacama Desert.

megh-097.title: The 1964 Alaska earthquake
megh-097.text: The ground shook for 4 minutes 38 seconds. The Mw 9.2–9.3 quake that struck southern Alaska is the most powerful recorded in North America and second worldwide since 1900. Land rose across 520,000 km², by 13–15 m on Montague Island. The shaking collapsed weak clay beds left by ancient Lake Atna, setting off catastrophic landslides in Anchorage. Tsunamis ran up 67 m, and about 139 people died. Its seismic waves set water sloshing in seiches, standing waves in enclosed water, as far away as Puerto Rico.

megh-098.title: Wildlife populations plunge since 1970
megh-098.text: Monitored vertebrate wildlife populations fell by almost 70% on average after 1970. Agriculture and fishing drove most of it. Land-use change, overexploitation, climate change, pollution and invasive species all contributed, and migratory freshwater fish declined by 76%. Whole branches of life ended. In 1987 the death of the last Kauaʻi ʻōʻō ended an entire bird family, the Hawaiian honeyeaters. In the Yangtze, the Chinese paddlefish was last recorded in 2003, and the baiji river dolphin was declared extinct in 2006, the loss of a whole genus.

megh-101.title: A chytrid fungus kills off frogs
megh-101.text: Costa Rica's golden toad was last seen in 1989. It was one victim of chytridiomycosis, a fungal disease spread by travel and the wildlife trade. The disease has caused steep declines in over 500 amphibian species and perhaps 90 extinctions. Australia's gastric-brooding frogs were gone by the mid-1980s. The chytrid Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis has spread across Australia, New Zealand, Central America and Africa.

megh-100.title: Arctic sea ice shrinks
megh-100.text: In 2012 the September minimum of Arctic sea ice hit a record 3.39 million km², beating the 2007 record of 4.16 million km². Satellites have tracked the ice since 1979, and it has declined by over 50%. The loss accelerated to 4.7% per decade in the early 21st century. Old, thick ice is disappearing fastest. Ice at least four years old fell from 26% of the cover in 1988 to 7% by 2013, and ice thickness dropped 66% over six decades. Since 1979 the Arctic has warmed nearly four times faster than the global average. The loss feeds on itself: sea ice lost between 1979 and 2011 caused radiative forcing equal to a quarter of CO2 emissions over the same years.

megh-102.title: Mount St. Helens erupts in 1980
megh-102.text: On 18 May 1980, Mount St. Helens erupted catastrophically, the most significant eruption in the contiguous US in recorded history. It was a VEI 5 event of about 1.2–1.3 km³. Its flank collapsed into a huge debris avalanche, now the reference case for spotting such collapses at volcanoes such as Mount Bandai and Parinacota. Ash dusted land from British Columbia to Manitoba. Ferns recolonized the devastated ground first, a fern spike like the one after the dinosaur extinction.

megh-103.title: The ozone layer thins and a hole opens
megh-103.text: Antarctic spring ozone fell by up to 70%, a loss first reported in 1985. From the late 1970s, stratospheric ozone thinned worldwide, with a far deeper springtime loss over the poles: the Antarctic ozone hole. Manufactured chlorofluorocarbons, halons and related refrigerants, solvents and propellants were the main cause. Inside the polar vortex, over half the lower-stratospheric ozone is destroyed each spring. Mid-latitude ozone fell below pre-1980 values between 1980 and 1996, and Arctic losses reached 30% in the coldest winters and springs. Stronger ultraviolet-B under thinned ozone cuts plant productivity by about 6%. The hole has at times reached parts of Australia, Chile and Argentina.

megh-104.title: El Chichón warms the northern winter
megh-104.text: In spring 1982, long-dormant El Chichón in Chiapas, Mexico, produced three Plinian eruptions within a week. The VEI 5 eruption put 7 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide and 20 million tonnes of particles into the stratosphere, which circled Earth in three weeks. Its aerosols brought an unexpected result: winter warming in North America, Europe and Siberia in 1982–83. Alaska, Greenland and China ran colder than normal.

megh-105.title: Pinatubo cools the world in 1991
megh-105.text: World temperatures fell about 0.5 °C in 1991–1993 after one eruption. Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted on 15 June 1991, a VEI 6 event and the second-largest land eruption of the 20th century after Novarupta in 1912. Its ash column rose 35 km. It put more particles into the stratosphere than any eruption since Krakatoa in 1883. It released 17–20 megatonnes of sulfur dioxide, and the aerosols spread a global sulfuric-acid haze. Ozone depletion temporarily rose sharply, and 1992 brought a Summer that Wasn't across the United States. The summit collapsed into a 2.5 km caldera, later filled by Lake Pinatubo. Rain-driven lahars flooded the surrounding lowlands.

megh-106.title: Sea-level rise speeds up in the satellite era
megh-106.text: In 2016, flooding of Bramble Cay wiped out its melomys, a small rodent. Declared extinct in 2019, it was the first mammal lost to human-caused sea-level rise. Satellite altimeters, flying since TOPEX/Poseidon in 1992, measured 7.5 cm of rise from 1993 to 2017. The rate reached 4.62 mm a year in 2013–2022. From 1993 to 2018, melting ice sheets and glaciers supplied 44% of the rise, and thermal expansion of warming seawater 42%. Greenland's contribution grew from 0.07 mm a year in 1992–1997 to 0.68 mm a year in 2012–2017.

megh-108.title: Greenland's ice loss accelerates
megh-108.text: In 2021, rain fell for 13 hours at the 3,216 m Summit Station, where it had never rained before. Greenland's ice sheet is melting faster. Jakobshavn Isbræ, its largest outlet glacier, switched to rapid mass loss after 1997, as warming North Atlantic water melted glacier fronts from below. Annual ice loss from the whole sheet accelerated to about 187 Gt in 2000–2010 and 286 Gt in 2010–2018. In July 2012, melt reached 97% of the ice sheet's surface, a melt unmatched since 1889. That year's net loss of 464 Gt set a record. An even larger melt in 2019 brought a record net loss of 586 Gt, with about 600 Gt of ice lost in just two months.

megh-109.title: 1998: the first global coral bleaching
megh-109.text: Coral bleaching happens when heat-stressed corals expel the algae that live in them and turn white. In 1998 the first globally recognized bleaching event struck, with 21% of reefs under bleaching-level heat stress. A very strong 1997–98 El Niño drove it, warming Indian Ocean waters by 2 °C. 1998 became the warmest year then on record. Belize's barrier reef had its first recorded mass bleaching, and the Great Barrier Reef its first major bleaching event. Since the early 1980s, mass bleaching has grown sharply in frequency and severity worldwide, driven by marine heatwaves.

megh-110.title: The warming 'hiatus' of 1998–2013
megh-110.text: From 1998 to 2013, negative phases of the Pacific decadal and Atlantic multidecadal oscillations briefly slowed surface warming. These are slow natural swings in ocean temperature. The slowdown is less pronounced in current datasets than in those available in 2012, and the claim that warming stopped in 1998 is disputed. It ended after 2012: every year from 2015 on was warmer than any before, and 2024 exceeded 1.5 °C.

megh-111.title: Mass bleaching returns to the Great Barrier Reef
megh-111.text: Over half of the Great Barrier Reef's coral cover was lost between 1995 and 2017. Marine heatwaves caused mass coral bleaching there in 1998, 2002, 2006, 2016, 2017 and 2020, with another event confirmed in March 2022. Many breeding adults died in the 2016–17 bleaching. Warming is already bleaching coral reefs worldwide, habitats that sustain high biodiversity.

megh-112.title: The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami
megh-112.text: Within seven minutes, the seafloor off Sumatra rose up to 5 m and shifted 11 m sideways. On 26 December 2004, the boundary between the Indian and Burma plates slipped in a megathrust earthquake of magnitude 9.1–9.3. More than 1,600 km of the fault ruptured. It was the second- or third-most powerful quake since 1900, releasing about one-eighth of all seismic moment from 1906 to 2005. The tsunami reached 35 m near Banda Aceh and killed approximately 229,800 people around the Indian Ocean. It was not the first. Deposits on Phra Thong, Thailand, record at least three earlier major tsunamis in 2,800 years, the latest about 700 years ago.

megh-114.title: The 2010 Chile earthquake
megh-114.text: On 27 February 2010, a magnitude 8.8 earthquake struck central Chile. Its waves set off seiches as far away as Louisiana. Nearby, the Caldera del Atuel and other volcanic centres subsided after the quake, much as the volcano in {{ref:megh-095}} had stirred after the 1960 quake.

megh-115.title: The 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami
megh-115.text: The tsunami reached up to 40.5 m at Miyako and swept up to 10 km inland. On 11 March 2011, a magnitude 9.0–9.1 undersea megathrust earthquake struck off Honshu, as the Pacific plate subducted beneath the Okhotsk microplate. The worst-hit areas of Tōhoku shook for about six minutes. Japan's most powerful recorded quake, it released about 93% of the moment estimated to have built up there since 1926. Its seismic waves crossed 8,000 km in under 30 minutes, raising seiches about 1.5–1.8 m high in Norway. 19,759 people died, and three Fukushima Daiichi reactors melted down.

megh-117.title: The Chelyabinsk airburst
megh-117.text: On 15 February 2013, an asteroid about 20 m across exploded over Chelyabinsk, Russia, in an airburst of around 500 kilotons. It was the largest airburst observed with modern instruments. It shattered windows, injured over 1,000 people and scattered meteorites. Its similar dynamics reinforced the view that the Tunguska blast of {{ref:megh-081}} was a meteoroid exploding high in the air.

megh-118.title: The global coral bleaching of 2014–2017
megh-118.text: In 2016, bleaching killed 29 to 50% of the Great Barrier Reef's coral. Near Port Douglas, over half the bleached corals died. Record ocean heat during the 2014–2017 El Niño caused the longest and most destructive coral bleaching event then known. Bleaching in 2014–2016 killed coral on an unprecedented scale. Reefs making up three-quarters of the world's reef systems were severely bleached.

megh-119.title: Reykjanes wakes after 800 years
megh-119.text: After nearly 800 years of quiet, volcanic and earthquake activity resumed on Iceland's Reykjanes Peninsula from 2020. Fagradalsfjall erupted on 19 March 2021. In late 2023, a 15 km magma intrusion opened a subsiding graben, a sunken block of crust, beneath Grindavík and forced the town's evacuation. Nine Sundhnúkur fissure eruptions followed through August 2025. They were small and effusive, VEI 1, but experts suggested the activity may mark the start of decades of volcanism.

megh-120.title: Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai blows its top
megh-120.text: Its plume reached 58 km, into the mesosphere. The submarine Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai volcano had been erupting since December 2021, and on 15 January 2022 it exploded. It was the largest eruption since Pinatubo, rated at least VEI 5, and the largest atmospheric explosion recorded by modern instruments. Pressure waves raced around the globe, and a Pacific-wide tsunami followed. It lofted 146 million tons of seawater, a tenth of the stratosphere's water vapour, enough to warm Earth's surface temporarily.

megh-121.title: The fourth global coral bleaching
megh-121.text: From January 2023 to September 2025, bleaching-level heat reached about 84% of the world's reef area. A fourth global coral bleaching event began in February 2023, and in April 2024 NOAA confirmed it as the largest yet. Bleaching struck at least 83 countries and territories. On the Great Barrier Reef, hard-coral cover fell by up to 30.6% from 2024 to 2025, the largest single-year drops since 1986 in two regions.

megh-122.title: 2024, the warmest year on record
megh-122.text: 2024 was the warmest year since regular tracking began in 1850, at +1.60 °C, well above the 1.5 °C mark. It followed 2023, already 1.48 °C above the 1850–1900 average and declared the warmest year on record as soon as it ended. The years 2015–2025 included all eleven warmest since 1850. The 2016–2025 decade averaged 1.26 °C above pre-industrial. NOAA data rank 2025 as the third-warmest year on record, behind 2024 and 2023.

megh-123.title: The Anthropocene epoch is voted down
megh-123.text: In 2024, after 15 years of deliberation, stratigraphers voted down by a wide margin the proposal to make the Anthropocene a formal epoch after the Holocene. Its shallow sediment record and very recent start date weighed against it. The ICS and IUGS then confirmed the rejection by a near-unanimous vote. The term stays in wide informal use for human impact on the Earth system. Its validity as a scientific term remains disputed.

megh-124.title: The 2025 Kamchatka earthquake
megh-124.text: In 2025, another giant megathrust earthquake, of magnitude 8.8, struck the Kamchatka coast. There the Pacific plate subducts along the Kuril–Kamchatka Trench, the same boundary that broke in {{ref:megh-091}}.

megh-063.text: A boundary where one tectonic plate dives beneath another.

megh-097.text: A standing wave that sloshes back and forth in an enclosed body of water.

megh-109.text: The whitening of heat-stressed corals that expel the algae living in them.

megh-119.text: A block of crust that has dropped down between faults.
